106.title: Om gam ganapataye
106.hook: Ganesha's mantra; why even Shiva begins with him
106.carry: begin with ganesha: gam, his seed sound
106.howItsDone: Hindus commonly invoke Ganesha before beginning anything: a puja, a journey, a business, a wedding, an exam. Om Gam Ganapataye Namah is chanted in japa, often 108 times, in many regions especially on Wednesdays and on Ganesh Chaturthi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Appar's floating stone and the panchakshara, Om Namah Shivaya. Your line was om namah shivaya: Shiva's name is a refuge. Today, Shiva's son, and the mantra for starting things.
screen: `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA: SHIVA'S NAME IS A REFUGE.`

segments.voice: A new shop opens in Delhi, and before the first customer walks in, there's a small picture of Ganesha by the till with a garland on it. A student in Chennai writes Shri Ganesh at the top of an exam paper before the first answer. A new car gets a little Ganesha on the dashboard. Whatever is starting, he's there first. You've heard how Shiva promised his son would be worshipped first. Here's the day the promise was tested, on Shiva himself.
screen: `A NEW SHOP, A NEW EXAM.` → `A NEW CAR.` → `GANESHA IS THERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Ganesha's own Purana tells it, and a temple in Tamil Nadu is named for it. Shiva sets out to destroy Tripura, three flying cities of demons that only a single arrow could ever bring down. The whole universe becomes his war chariot: the earth for its body, the sun and moon for its wheels. And Shiva, in a hurry, doesn't stop to honor Ganesha. The axle snaps. The great god stands there with his bow, going nowhere. So Shiva does what everyone else does. He honors his son first. The chariot rolls, and the three cities fall to one arrow. Even the god who made the promise keeps it. That's why so many Hindu rituals open with Ganesha, even a puja to another god. One of his names is Vighneshvara, lord of obstacles: he removes them, and some say he also places them, when a road shouldn't be taken yet. And the way many people ask is this mantra: Om Gam Ganapataye Namah. Om, the sound of everything. Gam, a bija, a seed syllable. In Hindu mantra practice, a bija isn't a word about a god; many hold that it carries the god inside it, the way a seed holds a tree. Gam is Ganesha's seed. Ganapataye: to Ganapati, lord of the hosts. Namah: I bow. So the Ganesha on the dashboard, the Shri Ganesh at the top of a page, the gam said quietly before a first day or a hard conversation: it's the lesson of the broken axle. Begin with Ganesha.
screen: `EVEN SHIVA FORGOT ONCE.` · `THE AXLE SNAPS.` · `VIGHNESHVARA, LORD OF OBSTACLES.` · `GAM — GANESHA'S SEED SYLLABLE.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH GANESHA: GAM.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one thing you're about to begin, this week, tomorrow, even the next hour. Then, on beads or finger joints, do japa twenty-seven times: Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, slowly, letting the gam land softly, like something set down at a doorway. If you don't pray, let it be sound and counting, with the thing you're beginning in view, and at twenty-seven, rest.
Bija, a seed syllable that holds a deity inside it: gam, Ganesha's seed, in the mantra Om Gam Ganapataye, said before beginnings.
Take this with you: begin with Ganesha, gam, his seed sound. Even Shiva starts there. Day one hundred six, done.

107.title: Hare Krishna
107.howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, including members of ISKCON, chant the Hare Krishna maha-mantra daily on beads, often sixteen rounds of 108, and sing it together in kirtan with drums and cymbals, at home, in temples and in the street.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bija: gam, Ganesha's seed, and the day Shiva's axle broke. Your line was begin with Ganesha: gam, his seed sound. Today, a mantra that's meant to be sung.

A group walks down a city street, in London or New York or Sydney, in saffron and white, with a drum and small hand cymbals, singing. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna. People stare, or smile, or cross the street. It can look like something new. It isn't. That same song filled the streets of a town in Bengal in the fifteen-hundreds, sung by a man who, his followers say, danced until he fell to the ground. And the words themselves are older still.
screen: `A DRUM AND CYMBALS DOWNTOWN.` → `IT LOOKS NEW. IT ISN'T.` → `A TOWN IN BENGAL, THE 1500S.`

segments.voice: Here are the words. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Sixteen words, only three names. Krishna, the one you followed from the prison at midnight to the chariot. Rama, the prince who came home to a city of lamps. And Hare, which many devotees understand as calling on Hara, Radha, the love and energy of God, and which others hear as a form of Hari, Vishnu, the one who takes away. That's the maha-mantra, the great mantra. It appears, with the Rama half first, in a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, which says that in this age, the simplest way across is the name. Then, in the early fifteen-hundreds, in Navadvip in Bengal, came Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. His followers remember him as Krishna himself, come as a devotee, taking the names out of quiet rooms and into the street. Singing together, with drums and cymbals, is called sankirtan, and Chaitanya made it the heart of the practice. Why out loud? Here's the teaching: in Chaitanya's tradition, the holy name isn't just a word about Krishna. It is not different from Krishna himself, present in sound. So singing it together is the practice for this age, and sung, it reaches everyone in earshot, even the ones crossing the street. In 1965, a monk in his line, an elderly man named A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, arrived in New York with almost nothing. Before long he was singing it in a city park. That's where the group you saw comes from. Sankirtan: God's name, sung together.
screen: `SIXTEEN WORDS, THREE NAMES.` · `THE SIMPLEST WAY ACROSS.` · `CHAITANYA TAKES IT TO THE STREET.` · `THE NAME IS KRISHNA, IN SOUND.` · then, large: `SANKIRTAN: GOD'S NAME, SUNG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: This one isn't whispered: if you're somewhere you can, sing it softly, to any simple tune or on one note. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Once through is one round; keep going, and tap your knee for a drum if you like. If you don't pray, let it simply be singing, and notice what singing does that speaking doesn't; if you can't make noise, mouth the words.

108.title: The Gayatri at dawn
108.hook: Rama woken for the dawn prayer; sandhya
108.carry: sandhya: the gayatri, kept at dawn
108.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant the Gayatri at dawn and dusk as part of sandhya worship, often facing the sun and offering water; traditionally it is taught at the upanayana (sacred thread) ceremony, while many modern teachers and movements share it with all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hare Krishna, Chaitanya's song in the street. Your line was sankirtan: God's name, sung together. Today, a quieter verse, and a teacher who wakes a prince before sunrise.

Before dawn, on the steps down to the river at Varanasi, a man stands waist-deep in the water, facing east. He cups water in his hands, and as the first edge of the sun comes up, he lifts it and says a few lines under his breath. Far away in New Jersey, a boy with a new thread across his chest sets an alarm for the same hour. Same words, far older than either of them: the Gayatri. You learned on day three what it asks for. Today, why it's kept at dawn.
screen: `A MAN IN THE RIVER, FACING EAST.` → `A BOY SETS AN ALARM.` → `WHY DAWN?`

segments.voice: The Ramayana has a quiet moment that shows it. The sage Vishvamitra, the seer tradition credits with the Gayatri, has taken two boys from the palace, Rama and his brother Lakshmana. They sleep on a riverbank. Before sunrise the old sage bends over them and wakes them, in a verse that still opens the morning song at many temples: Rama, Kausalya's blessed son, the eastern sandhya, the dawn, is coming. Get up; the day's rites to the gods are waiting. And the princes rise, bathe in the river, offer water, and do their japa. Many teachers say what they chanted was the Gayatri. Here's the teaching. Did you hear the word? Sandhya: the junction, where night meets day, and the name of the dawn prayer itself. Traditionally the Gayatri is given to a child at the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, and from then on it's kept at the junctions of the day: facing the rising sun, offering water from cupped hands, asking the sun's light to wake the mind. Traditions differ on who chants it. Many keep it for those who have received the thread; many modern teachers and movements open it to everyone. Both views are held by devout Hindus; its meaning in English belongs to anyone. Now notice Rama. In the tradition he's God born human, and still his teacher wakes him in the dark to pray. The Gayatri isn't saved for a crisis. It's kept like a promise, at the same hour, before anything else gets the mind. Sandhya: the Gayatri, kept at dawn.
screen: `RAMA, THE DAWN IS COMING.` · `THE PRINCES RISE AND PRAY.` · `SANDHYA: WHERE NIGHT MEETS DAY.` · `WHO CHANTS IT: TRADITIONS DIFFER.` · then, large: `SANDHYA: THE GAYATRI, KEPT AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Sit facing a window if you can, or picture the sun just coming up. If your tradition welcomes you to chant it, say the last line softly, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat; if not, hold its meaning in English: light, illuminate the mind. Say it once, then hold it the way you'd hold your face toward the morning sun, and say it again when your attention drifts.
The Gayatri. A verse to the sun who stirs everything awake, kept at the junctions of the day, asking it to light up our minds.
Carry this: sandhya, the Gayatri, kept at dawn. Even Rama got up in the dark for it. That's day one hundred eight.

109.title: Silent japa
109.hook: Valmiki's mara-mara; the mantra without the mouth
109.carry: japa goes inward until it says itself
109.howItsDone: Hindu practitioners do japa aloud, whispered or silently in the mind; many meditation lineages teach so-ham (hamsa) with the breath, describing the ajapa japa as the mantra the breath repeats on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri, kept at dawn the way Rama kept it. Your line was sandhya: the Gayatri, kept at dawn. Today, the mantra goes quiet.

You know how a song gets stuck in your head? You didn't decide to hum it. You're brushing your teeth and there it is, playing by itself. Annoying, when it's an advertising jingle. But what if it were something you'd chosen? Hindu tradition noticed this long ago, and it tells a story about a robber whose mantra started saying itself.
screen: `A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `WHAT IF YOU CHOSE THE SONG?` → `A ROBBER'S MANTRA.`

segments.voice: Remember Valmiki, the robber from day seven, who sat so long an anthill grew over him? A much-loved later telling says what he was doing in there. The sage gave him a name to repeat: Rama. But the robber couldn't get it out; the holy name stuck in a mouth used to threats. So the sage said: then say it backwards. Mara. Mara, mara, mara. Say it fast and listen: maramaramara turns into rama, rama, rama. The name was saying itself, and he sat so still the ants built over him. Here's the teaching behind it. Japa, repeating a sacred name, comes three ways. Out loud, as you did with Hare Krishna, is vachika. Whispered, lips moving, barely a sound, is upamshu. Silent, only in the mind, is manasika. Many old texts and teachers rank the silent one highest: the quieter it gets, the deeper it goes in, with no sound to lean on. And past that is ajapa. The a at the front means not: not-repeating. Many yoga teachers say the breath already carries a mantra, a soft so on the in-breath and ham on the out: so-ham, I am that. You can't force ajapa. You start with silent japa, let go, and listen for it. So when a grandmother's lips move without a sound all the way to the store, she isn't mumbling. She's on Valmiki's road: from the lips, inward, until the name says itself.
screen: `VALMIKI: MARA, MARA, MARA…` · `…RAMA, RAMA, RAMA.` · `SPOKEN, WHISPERED, SILENT.` · `AJAPA — NOT-REPEATING.` · then, large: `JAPA GOES INWARD UNTIL IT SAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Settle into your breath and say your mantra silently, the one that fits or simply so-ham: so as you breathe in, ham as you breathe out, no lips, no whisper. After a while, stop saying it on purpose and just listen for the so and the ham in the breath. If you lose it, start saying it again, gently, and let go again.
Ajapa. Not-repeating. The mantra that goes on by itself, carried on the breath: so on the way in, ham on the way out.
Keep this one: japa goes inward until it says itself. Valmiki's name turned around on its own. Day one hundred nine.

110.title: A full round
110.hook: Rama gives Hanuman 108; the mala's full round
110.carry: the mala: one full round of 108
110.howItsDone: Hindus doing japa commonly use a mala of 108 beads plus a larger meru bead, moving one bead per mantra with the thumb and middle finger, and turning back at the meru rather than crossing it; one full round is 108 repetitions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ajapa, and Valmiki's name that turned itself around. Your line was japa goes inward until japa goes inward until it says itself. Today, the end of mantra week, and your first full round.
screen: `JAPA GOES INWARD UNTIL JAPA GOES INWARD UNTIL IT SAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Pick up a japa mala, a string of prayer beads, and count. Very often: one hundred and eight. Plus one more, bigger, set apart, often with a tassel. Gods have lists of 108 names, recited as one long litany of praise. Some sacred places are counted in sets of 108. The number keeps turning up. Ask people why, and you'll get plenty of confident answers, and they won't match.
screen: `108 BEADS, PLUS ONE.` → `108 NAMES, 108 PLACES.` → `MANY ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Nobody knows for certain why 108; people give many answers, and they don't match. But one text shows how it came to mean complete. It's a conversation in Ayodhya, after the war. Hanuman, who leapt the ocean and carried the mountain, sits at Rama's feet and asks what every seeker asks: how does anyone get free? Rama answers in a short text called the Muktika Upanishad. One Upanishad is enough, he says, if you truly take it in. If not, ten. If not, thirty-two. And if not, here are a hundred and eight, the full set: take these in, and you'll be free. So 108 became one of the tradition's ways of saying the whole. There are lists of 108 names for Vishnu, for Shiva, for the Goddess, for Ganesha. And there's the japa mala: 108 beads, plus one big bead, the meru, named for the mountain at the center of the world, and also called the guru bead. Here's how a round works. Hold the mala in your right hand, over the middle finger, and pull each bead toward you with your thumb, one bead per mantra. Many teachers say to keep the index finger off the beads. When you come back to the meru, you don't cross it; many explain that you don't step over the guru. For another round, turn the mala around and go back the way you came. And that's the week: Ganesha's seed, the name sung together, the Gayatri at dawn, the name going inward. Now one full round of 108: a whole offering, start to finish.

111.title: The honored guest
111.hook: Dhanna's rock; a shelf of five things for God
111.carry: the murti is an honored guest
111.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small shrine, from a whole puja room to a kitchen shelf, with an image or picture of the family's deities, a lamp, flowers, a bell and water, where daily puja is offered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meru, and your first full round. Your line was the mala: one full round of 108. This week, the practice gets a home. Literally.

In many Hindu homes there's a small shrine. In a big house it might be a whole room; in a student apartment, a shelf above the desk. In a lot of kitchens it's a little alcove near the stove, with a picture of Krishna leaning against the spice jars and a lamp lit every morning for as long as anyone remembers. It's called the mandir, the temple, or the puja room, even when it's only a shelf. And a simple one can come down to five things.
screen: `A ROOM, OR A SHELF.` → `KRISHNA BY THE SPICE JARS.` → `IT COMES DOWN TO FIVE THINGS.`

segments.voice: Who lives on that shelf? Dhanna was a farm boy in Rajasthan, and the story told of him goes like this. He watched a brahmin worship a sacred stone every morning, and begged for one of his own. To get rid of him, the brahmin handed him an ordinary rock. Dhanna took it home, set it in a clean place, and at mealtime put his own food in front of it and waited for God to eat. God didn't. So Dhanna didn't either. Days went by, the boy hungry, stubborn and sure. And in the story, God came and ate from his plate. A plain rock, offered to with that much love, had become a home for God. Here's the teaching. Many Hindus understand a murti, the image on the shrine, as a place where the divine is truly present, and welcome it as an honored guest; others see it as a focus for the mind; both are held. That's why the five simple things are what a good host offers. One, the image itself, the guest. Two, a lamp, for light. Three, a flower, something beautiful, given away. Four, a bell, rung to begin, to call the attention of the divine, many say, and your own. Five, water, the first thing you'd offer anyone who walks in. Nothing costly; Dhanna's rock cost nothing. Keep it clean and a little apart, and remember: a shelf you pass every morning beats a perfect room you never enter. The murti is an honored guest.
screen: `DHANNA'S ORDINARY ROCK.` · `HE WOULDN'T EAT UNTIL GOD DID.` · `THE MURTI — AN HONORED GUEST.` · `IMAGE, LAMP, FLOWER, BELL, WATER.` · then, large: `THE MURTI IS AN HONORED GUEST.`

segments.voice: Choose a place, a shelf, the corner of a dresser, a windowsill, and clear it. Gather what you have: an image or a picture that means something to you, a candle or tea light, a flower or a leaf from outside, anything that rings, even a spoon on a glass, and a small cup of water, and set them down slowly. If you can't do it right now, picture exactly where it will go, then sit in front of it and breathe.
Five objects. An image, a lamp, a flower, a bell, and water: what a good host sets out for the guest on a home shrine.
Take this with you: the murti is an honored guest. Dhanna's rock was enough, and a shelf is plenty. One hundred eleven days in.

112.title: The lamp
112.hook: Agni hides; why the lamp is lit first and greeted
112.carry: the lamp's light is greeted as god
112.howItsDone: Many Hindu households light a small lamp, often a clay diya with a cotton wick in ghee or oil, at the home shrine at dawn and at dusk, and many greet its light with a short Sanskrit verse beginning shubham karoti kalyanam, often followed by deepa jyoti parabrahma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five objects on a shelf, and Dhanna's ordinary rock. Your line was the murti is an honored guest. Today, the second object.

The power goes out at night. The fridge stops humming. Everyone goes quiet. Somebody fumbles in a drawer, finds a candle, strikes a match. And the whole room changes. Faces come back. People talk more softly, as if the little flame were listening. Many Hindu homes light a flame on purpose, every evening, even when the power is fine. It's the second object on the shelf, and it comes with one of the oldest stories in Hinduism.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `ONE MATCH, AND THE ROOM CHANGES.` → `ONE OF HINDUISM'S OLDEST STORIES.`

segments.voice: In the oldest hymns, the Rig Veda, fire is a god: Agni, the one who carries every offering up to the gods. And one hymn tells how Agni ran away. He was afraid of the work; the fires before him, he says, had worn out in that service. So he hid, deep in the waters and the plants, and the offerings had no one to carry them. The gods went looking, found him, and coaxed him: come back. They promised him a share of the offerings and a life that wouldn't age. And Agni came out and took his place again, between the people and the gods. That's the flame in a Hindu home. The Sanskrit word for the lamp is deepa, from a root meaning to shine. Often it's a small clay diya with a cotton wick in ghee or oil, lit at dawn and at dusk, and often lit as puja begins. Many families greet it with a short verse beginning shubham karoti kalyanam, honoring the lamp's light for bringing what is good and pushing away what harms. Many go on: deepa jyoti parabrahma, the lamp's light is the supreme Brahman. That's the teaching. The flame isn't only a sign that God is near. Many Hindus greet the light itself as God, the one reality shining in everything, small enough to sit in a clay bowl. So it's lit first, and bowed to. And people point out one more thing: when one lamp lights another, it loses nothing. That's why, back on day five, arti was light passed hand to hand.
screen: `AGNI HIDES IN THE WATERS.` · `THE GODS COAX HIM BACK.` · `DEEPA — FROM A ROOT: TO SHINE.` · `DEEPA JYOTI PARABRAHMA.` · then, large: `THE LAMP'S LIGHT IS GREETED AS GOD.`

segments.voice: If it's safe, light a candle or a lamp somewhere steady, away from anything that can catch; if not, picture one. Let your eyes rest on the flame softly, without staring hard, and notice how it moves with your breath, the bright middle, the blue at the base. Then close your eyes for a moment, see if the shape of it stays, and open them: one flame, that's all.
Deepa. The lamp: a small flame, from a root meaning to shine, lit at the edges of the day and greeted as God.
Your line: the lamp's light is greeted as God. One flame, and it loses nothing when it's shared. Until tomorrow.
